Classification Binary classification is a supervised learning task in which each input sample is assigned to one of two possible classes. The class labels are usually represented as y ∈{−1, +1} or sometimes y ∈{0, 1}. In binary classification, the learning algorithm uses training data to learn a rule that predicts the class label of new samples. Each training example is written as (xi, yi) where xi ∈Rn is the feature vector and yi ∈{−1, +1} is the class label. The index i denotes the training example, with i = 1, 2, . . . , m.

Examples of Binary Classification Binary classification appears in many practical applications: • Email filtering: classifying messages as spam or not spam • Medical diagnosis: determining whether a disease is present or absent • Credit approval: deciding whether to approve or reject a loan • Quality control: identifying defective and non-defective products • Exam prediction: predicting whether a student will pass or fail © Kunal Kundu Asst. boundary. The prediction is based on a linear function of the input features. The decision function is f(x) = w⊤x + b where • x ∈Rn is the feature vector • w ∈Rn is the weight vector • b ∈R is the bias term • w⊤x = Pn j=1 wjxj is the dot product The value f(x) is called the decision score. Its sign determines the predicted class, and its magnitude is proportional to the distance from the decision boundary. Classification Rule The predicted class label ˆy is determined by the sign of the decision function: ˆy = ( +1 if w⊤x + b > 0 −1 if w⊤x + b < 0 If w⊤x + b = 0 the point lies exactly on the decision boundary.

In practice, this case is rare; the classification may be considered ambiguous or assigned arbitrarily to one class. Decision Boundary The decision boundary is the set of points satisfying w⊤x + b = 0. This equation defines a hyperplane that separates the feature space into two regions. • In two dimensions (n = 2), the boundary is a line: w1x1 + w2x2 + b = 0 • In three dimensions (n = 3), the boundary is a plane: w1x1 + w2x2 + w3x3 + b = 0 • In higher dimensions (n ≥4), the boundary is called a hyperplane: w⊤x + b = 0 The weight vector w is perpendicular to the decision boundary and determines its orientation. The bias b determines its position relative to the origin. © Kunal Kundu Asst.

Features with larger magnitudes can dominate the decision function. It is common practice to standardize features to have zero mean and unit variance before training. • Feature engineering: Linear models cannot capture nonlinear relationships unless appropriate feature transformations (e.g., polynomial features, interactions) are provided as inputs.

• Class imbalance: When one class significantly outnumbers the other, the decision boundary may be biased. Techniques such as class weighting or resampling can help address this issue. Advantages of Linear Classification • Simplicity: Easy to understand and implement. • Interpretability: The weight vector directly indicates the importance of each feature. • Efficiency: Fast to train and evaluate, even on large datasets. • Well-studied: Solid mathematical foundation with convex optimization guarantees. Limitations • Linearity assumption: Cannot capture complex nonlinear patterns without feature engineering.

• Feature dependence: Performance depends strongly on the quality and relevance of input fea- tures. • Sensitivity: May be sensitive to outliers in some formulations. Relation to Other Algorithms Several important machine learning algorithms are based on the linear classification model: • Linear Support Vector Machines (SVM): Find the hyperplane that maximizes the margin between classes. • Logistic Regression: Models class probabilities using the logistic function. • Perceptron: Online learning algorithm that updates weights upon misclassification. • Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA): Assumes Gaussian class distributions and finds the optimal separating hyperplane. © Kunal Kundu Asst.

input sample belongs to one of more than two classes. Unlike binary classification, where there are only two classes, multi-class classification involves three or more classes. Let the class labels be y ∈{1, 2, 3, . . . , K} where K ≥3 is the number of classes. Each training example is written as (xi, yi) where xi ∈Rn is the feature vector and yi is the class label. Model for Multi-class Classification A linear model for multi-class classification assigns a score to each class. For class k, the score is fk(x) = w⊤ k x + bk where wk and bk are the parameters for class k.

The predicted class is the one with the highest score: ˆy = arg max k fk(x) Confusion Matrix for Multi-class Classification A confusion matrix summarizes the performance of a classifier. The model assumes that the output can be expressed as a weighted sum of the input features. Let the input feature vector be x = (x1, x2, . . . , xn) ∈Rn. A general linear model is written as y = w1x1 + w2x2 + · · · + wnxn + b where x1, x2, . . . , xn are input features, w1, w2, . . . , wn ∈R are model weights, b ∈R is the bias term, and y ∈R is the predicted output. The weights determine the importance of each feature.

A larger absolute value of a weight indicates that the corresponding feature has a stronger influence on the prediction. Meaning of Rn The symbol R denotes the set of all real numbers. The notation Rn represents the set of all vectors that contain n real numbers. Thus, a vector in Rn has the form (x1, x2, . . . , xn) where each xi ∈R. Vector Representation Linear models are often written using vector notation because it provides a compact mathematical representation. Let x =   x1 x2 ... xn  ∈Rn, w =   w1 w2 ... wn  ∈Rn. The linear model can then be written as y = w⊤x + b where w⊤denotes the transpose of the weight vector. The term w⊤x represents the dot product w⊤x = n X i=1 wixi. Linear Decision Boundary In classification problems, linear models create a linear decision boundary.

This boundary separates the feature space into regions that correspond to different class labels. In two dimensions the decision boundary is a straight line w1x1 + w2x2 + b = 0. In three dimensions the boundary becomes a plane w1x1 + w2x2 + w3x3 + b = 0. In higher dimensions the boundary is called a hyperplane w⊤x + b = 0. This hyperplane divides the feature space into two regions. They are easy to interpret because each weight represents the contribution of a feature. They are computationally efficient and can be trained quickly even on large datasets. The mathematical formulation is simple and the optimization problems are usually convex, which guarantees a unique optimal solution. Limitations of Linear Models Linear models also have limitations. They cannot represent complex nonlinear relationships unless additional feature transformations are introduced.

Their performance depends strongly on the quality of the input features. They can also be sensitive to outliers. Many machine learning algorithms are based on linear models. Examples include Linear Regression, Logistic Regression, and Linear Support Vector Machines. 4 Linear Support Vector Machines (SVM) Introduction The Support Vector Machine (SVM) is a supervised learning algorithm used mainly for classification problems. Linear SVM attempts to find a hyperplane that separates two classes. The main idea of SVM is to choose the separating hyperplane that maximizes the distance between the classes. This distance is called the margin.

Points on one side of the hyperplane belong to class +1. Points on the other side belong to class −1. Margin The margin is the distance between the separating hyperplane and the closest data points from each class. Two parallel hyperplanes define the margin boundaries w⊤x + b = 1 w⊤x + b = −1. The distance between these two hyperplanes is margin = 2 ∥w∥. A smaller value of ∥w∥produces a larger margin. Support Vectors The data points that lie closest to the margin boundaries are called support vectors. These points determine the position of the separating hyperplane. If the support vectors move, the decision boundary also changes.

4.1 Hard-Margin SVM In some datasets the two classes can be perfectly separated by a linear boundary. This situation is called linear separability. In such cases it is possible to draw a hyperplane that correctly classifies all training points. However, many different separating hyperplanes may exist. Some of these hyperplanes pass very close to the data points, while others leave a larger gap between the classes. Support Vector Machines choose the hyperplane that leaves the largest possible margin between the two classes. This model is called the hard-margin SVM because it does not allow any classification errors. Margin Constraints Recall that the separating hyperplane is w⊤x + b = 0.

The margin boundaries are defined as w⊤x + b = 1 and w⊤x + b = −1. For correctly classified points the following condition must hold: yi(w⊤xi + b) ≥1. This constraint ensures two things: • each point is classified correctly © Kunal Kundu Asst. Prof. (IT), GHRCEM 10

margin boundaries and become the support vectors. Why Optimization is Needed Many hyperplanes can separate the data. The goal of SVM is to choose the one that maximizes the margin between the classes. The width of the margin is margin = 2 ∥w∥. Maximizing the margin is therefore equivalent to minimizing the norm of the weight vector. For mathematical convenience the squared norm is minimized instead. Hard-Margin Optimization Problem The SVM training problem becomes the following constrained optimization problem: min w,b 1 2∥w∥2 subject to yi(w⊤xi + b) ≥1, i = 1, . . . , m. The objective function 1 2∥w∥2 controls the margin size. Minimizing it produces the maximum-margin hyperplane.

The constraints ensure that all training samples are classified correctly. How the Optimization is Solved The above problem is a convex quadratic optimization problem. Such problems have a unique global optimum. In practice the optimization is solved using methods such as • Quadratic Programming • Sequential Minimal Optimization (SMO) • Gradient-based optimization methods These algorithms compute the optimal parameters w and b that define the separating hyperplane. An important result of the optimization is that only a small number of training points influence the final solution. These points are the support vectors. All other points do not affect the decision boundary. © Kunal Kundu Asst.

linear boundary. In many real datasets this assumption is not realistic. Data may contain noise, measurement errors, or overlapping class distributions. In such situations it may be impossible to find a hyperplane that correctly classifies every training point. Hard-margin SVM fails because its constraints require perfect separation. To address this limitation, the soft-margin SVM allows some training points to violate the margin constraints. The classifier still tries to maximize the margin, but it also allows a limited number of classification errors. Slack Variables Soft-margin SVM introduces additional variables called slack variables.

These variables measure how much a data point violates the margin constraint. For each training example a slack variable ξi is introduced such that ξi ≥0. The margin constraint becomes yi(w⊤xi + b) ≥1 −ξi. The value of ξi indicates the position of the point relative to the margin. • ξi = 0 : the point is correctly classified and lies outside the margin • 0 < ξi < 1 : the point lies inside the margin but remains correctly classified • ξi ≥1 : the point is misclassified Thus slack variables allow the classifier to tolerate margin violations. Soft-Margin Optimization The goal of SVM is still to find a hyperplane that maximizes the margin.

At the same time the classifier should minimize the number of margin violations. These two goals are combined into the following optimization problem: min w,b,ξ 1 2∥w∥2 + C m X i=1 ξi subject to yi(w⊤xi + b) ≥1 −ξi, ξi ≥0, i = 1, . . . , m. The objective function contains two terms. • The term 1 2∥w∥2 maximizes the margin. • The term P ξi penalizes margin violations. The optimization therefore balances margin size and classification errors. © Kunal Kundu Asst. Prof. (IT), GHRCEM 12

• Large C A large value of C strongly penalizes margin violations. The classifier tries to classify all training points correctly. This often produces a narrower margin and may lead to overfitting. • Small C A small value of C allows more violations of the margin. The classifier focuses more on maximizing the margin. Interpretation Using Loss Functions Soft-margin SVM can also be interpreted using the hinge loss. The hinge loss for a training example is Li = max(0, 1 −yi(w⊤xi + b)). This loss is zero for correctly classified points outside the margin.

It increases when a point moves inside the margin or becomes misclassified. Instead, it stores the training data and makes predictions by comparing new samples with stored instances. This approach is also called lazy learning because generalization occurs only when a prediction is required. The k-Nearest Neighbors (k-NN) method is a simple and widely used instance-based learning algorithm.

Basic Idea of k-NN The main idea of k-NN is as follows: • Given a new input point, find the k closest points in the training dataset. • Use the labels of these k neighbors to predict the class (for classification) or average their values (for regression). Choose the value of k. 2.

Compute the distance between the test point and all training points. 3. Select the k nearest neighbors. 4. Count the number of samples in each class among the neighbors. 5. Assign the class with the highest count. For regression, the prediction is the average of the target values of the k neighbors. Weighted k-NN In the basic k-NN method, all k neighbors contribute equally to the prediction. However, this may not be ideal because closer neighbors are usually more relevant than distant ones. Weighted k-NN assigns higher importance to nearer neighbors and lower importance to farther neighbors. Let x be the test point. Let Nk(x) denote the set of indices of the k nearest neighbors of x.

Each neighbor xi is assigned a weight wi based on its distance from x. A common choice is wi = 1 d(x, xi), where d(x, xi) is the distance between the test point and the i-th neighbor. Weighted classification rule: ˆy = arg max c X i∈Nk(x), yi=c wi where • ˆy is the predicted class • c represents a possible class label • Nk(x) is the set of k nearest neighbors • yi is the class label of the i-th neighbor • wi is the weight assigned to neighbor i This rule computes the total weight for each class and assigns the class with the largest total weight. Weighted regression: For regression, the predicted value is a weighted average: ˆy = P i∈Nk(x) wi yi P i∈Nk(x) wi .

Remarks: • Closer neighbors have larger weights and influence the prediction more strongly. • To avoid division by zero when distance is very small, a small constant ε can be added: wi = 1 d(x, xi) + ε. © Kunal Kundu Asst. Prof. (IT), GHRCEM 21

The core idea is that a group of models can produce better results than any single model, analogous to the ”wisdom of the crowd.” 6.1 Bias-Variance Trade-off Ensemble methods work by managing the bias-variance trade-off: • Bagging reduces variance by averaging predictions from models trained on different data subsets. • Boosting reduces bias by sequentially focusing on difficult examples. Bagging (Bootstrap Aggregating) Bagging trains multiple models on different subsets of the data. 1. Generate bootstrap samples from the dataset. 2. Train a model on each sample. 3. Combine predictions using voting (classification) or averaging (regression).

Models are trained independently and in parallel. Bias, Variance, and the Bias-Variance Trade-off When a machine learning model makes predictions, errors come from two main sources: • Bias: Error from oversimplifying the problem. High bias means the model misses important patterns (underfitting). • Variance: Error from being too sensitive to training data. High variance means the model learns noise instead of patterns (overfitting). The Trade-off Simple models have high bias but low variance. Complex models have low bias but high variance. The goal is to find the sweet spot where total error is minimized. © Kunal Kundu Asst. Prof. (IT), GHRCEM 33
